articles.title: Archaeologists are uncovering the meaning of a unique rock art site
articles.summary: Excavations in the Côa valley in Portugal, the world’s largest site of Palaeolithic open-air rock art, are yielding clues about how engravings of animals were seen by prehistoric hunter-gatherers
articles.content:
Excavations in the Côa valley in Portugal, the world’s largest site of Palaeolithic open-air rock art, are yielding clues about how engravings of animals were seen by prehistoric hunter-gatherers

Thierry Aubry highlights the outline of an aurochs motif on Penascosa Rock 3 Benjamin Taub

It’s 6am at the Penascosa rock art site in Portugal’s Côa valley, and under the raking glow of torchlight, a faded carving of an aurochs – a wild ox that lived during the last glacial period – suddenly comes into focus against the pre-dawn gloom. For three weeks, archaeologist Thierry Aubry from the Côa Park Foundation and his team have been digging beside the engravings in search of ancient tools that might help them understand the function of the valley’s oldest rock art. As we enter the final day of excavations, they have finally found what they are looking for: thumbnail-sized slivers of razor-sharp stone that were used as hunting weapons by prehistoric hunter-gatherers.

“This technology is typical from 26,000 years ago”, says Aubry in a voice tinged with excitement and relief. “It’s the first time we’ve found material this old next to the art.”

Finding these artefacts just a few metres from one of the most significant rock art panels in the entire Côa valley helps to demonstrate that art wasn’t just something our ancestors placed at remote sacred sites, but was “part of daily life”, says Luís Luís from the Côa Park Foundation.

Advertisement

Within the archaeological layers containing the stone bladelets, researchers also found the remains of other flaked tools as well as hearths, indicating that people made fire and used a range of utensils within touching distance of the engraved panel. Or, as Aubry puts it, “they were living inside the art”.

The stone tools at Penascosa provide vital clues about the social context in which the rock art was created and viewed, revealing how it shaped the encounters between groups of people who migrated to Côa to hunt and interact. “The most logical function is to transmit some mythology, but also to transmit some practical information for hunters,” says Aubry.

Thierry Aubry examines some 26,000-year-old bladelets from Penascosa Benjamin Taub

The Côa valley is the largest open-air collection of Palaeolithic rock art in the world. The engravings, which were first discovered in 1991, are spread over some 17 kilometres of river valley. “Art preserves well in caves, but not in the open air,” says Luís. “But here in Côa, we have conditions that allowed open-air art to be preserved, because it’s a dry region and the local schist is very resistant to erosion.”

The discovery of these exposed motifs triggered what Luís calls a “Copernican revolution” in archaeology by proving that rock art wasn’t restricted to the dark underground settings associated with religion and ritual, but was often a very public phenomenon.

“The Côa valley discovery prompted people to search for similar stuff elsewhere, and now we know from the last 30 years of discoveries that, in fact, it must have been all over the place,” says João Zilhão at the University of Lisbon in Portugal, who set up the Côa Valley Archaeological Park in 1996. Since then, further open-air sites of Palaeolithic rock art have been identified across the Iberian peninsula and beyond, with stylistically similar engravings found as far away as the Nile valley.

At Côa, the earliest phase of rock art production corresponds to the transition between the Gravettian and Solutrean periods of the Upper Palaeolithic, some 26,000 to 27,000 years ago at the onset of the last glacial maximum. To understand why hunter-gatherers chose to fill this valley with engravings 10,000 years before the Lascaux cave paintings in France were made, researchers have spent the past three decades searching for signs of occupation during the late Gravettian at Penascosa.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Our Human Story Sign up to newsletter

“In 1995, everybody said it would be impossible to find this because it’s an open-air site and it’s right by a river, so everything will have been washed away [during flooding events],” says Aubry. “But if you don’t look, you don’t find.”

The first attempt to find evidence of an ancient campsite was overseen by Zilhão. Yet by the end of the last major round of excavations, which Aubry led in 2018, layers showing signs of human occupation still hadn’t been found. In 2025, however, a test pit dug right in front of Penascosa’s Rock 3 – which is engraved with a series of overlapping animal motifs – revealed a number of fire-damaged rocks and flaked stone tools that match the style of the late Gravettian and early Solutrean.

For the first time, the team had direct evidence of people sitting around fires and manufacturing survival technologies at Penascosa, just as the landscape was being monumentalised through rock art. “What this shows is that the hunter-gatherers of the Palaeolithic were just like the hunter-gatherers of today,” says Zilhão, referring to certain Aboriginal Australian communities who continue to use rock art in a similar way. “They decorated the territory they lived in.”

A reassembled tool made from three stone flakes from Penascosa, thought to be 26,500 years old Thierry Aubry / Fundação Côa Parque

Returning to Penascosa last month to excavate this prehistoric living room, the team uncovered buried slabs of schist that had once formed a natural overhang, beneath which ancient hunter-gatherers had taken shelter until the heat from their campfires caused it to collapse. Digging through the layers of time, the archaeologists unearthed a sequence of artefacts that traced the course of human history from the Palaeolithic all the way up to Roman times. Unlike western Europe’s famous painted caves, then, the Côa valley and its rock art didn’t remain sealed off from the ever-changing outside world, but provided a stage for the social dramas that shaped the lives of ancient Iberians for millennia.

Eventually reaching the 27,000-year-old Gravettian occupation layer just as time was running out on the dig, the archaeologists uncovered the evidence they needed to orient Penascosa – and its earliest engravings – within the social landscape of ancient Iberia.

“This flint comes from central Spain, at least 150 kilometres away,” says Aubry, holding a tiny bladelet from Penascosa. “But this flint is from central Portugal, 200 kilometres the other way,” he says of another bladelet that was found in the same deposit. The convergence of these far-flung materials at this one spot suggests that, 27,000 years ago, the Côa valley sat at the heart of a vast network of exchange that spanned half of Iberia.

“This also explains why the art here is so similar in style to what you see in northern Spain, or even as far as the Rhône valley in France,” says Zilhão. These similarities, he suggests, indicate that rock art functioned as “a shared code of representation” belonging to “a network of people that exchanged information, personnel and objects, forming a very widespread area of cultural homogeneity”.

Yet the Côa valley may have been more than just another node in this network. “This region is a natural border between the [Atlantic] coast and the Iberian interior, so we think it was an important meeting place for populations from these different areas,” says Luís. For decades, archaeologists at Côa have argued that the valley was a social aggregation site, where bands of hunter-gatherers from across the Iberian hinterland periodically came together to meet and hunt. “The lithic materials give us that information,” says Luís. “We no longer see these populations as isolated.”

The valley’s rock art can therefore be understood as a key component of the social world that gave rise to it, in which highly mobile bands of hunter-gatherers repeatedly came face to face at Côa. In other words, as Luís says, “the art was used in moments when distant groups came together”.

Thierry Aubry points out the individual animal motifs within a composition featuring multiple overlapping animals at Fariseu Benjamin Taub

To highlight the role that rock art may have played in these encounters, Aubry takes me to Fariseu, another of the valley’s decorated sites. Here, archaeologists have found evidence that hunter-gatherers repeatedly lived among the artworks – although, unlike at Penascosa, they are yet to discover occupation layers dating to the late Gravettian, when the site’s earliest engravings were made.

“It’s a story, with a beginning, a middle and an end – like 16th-century art,” says Aubry as we stand before one of Fariseu’s engraved panels. “But I don’t think it was meant for the people from here. It was for people coming from other regions.”

On the rock face is a repeating series of motifs consisting of four female aurochs, each accompanied by a calf and apparently moving towards the nearby river. “One function was probably to establish a relationship with these animals, to show to people from other places that you are from a particular group,” says Aubry. This notion chimes with one presented by other scholars, who suggest that the Côa valley artists may have used animal motifs to represent humans.

Yet these engraved narratives may also have conveyed information about large herbivores and how to hunt them. The aurochs calves, for example, all appear to be around 6 months old, leading Aubry to speculate that the composition may depict the animals’ behaviour “at a specific moment in the year”.

“I think the aggregation moment was probably a hunting moment,” he says. “So the transmission of mythology was the social function [of the rock art], but the hunting function was also essential.” Rather than separating the symbolic from the practical, then, the same images could have performed both functions at once.

“Obviously it’s very difficult to understand the meaning of the art, but it may have been part of a survival strategy,” says Luís. As travellers and locals met at Côa’s engraved sites, the images they created may have facilitated vital exchanges between bands of strangers while also enabling them to hunt together.

“Côa revolutionised everything, because it made many of us realise that this is normal Ice Age art,” says freelance archaeologist Paul Bahn, who isn’t involved in the excavation. “I always assumed that they were living very close to the art, if not in the art sites themselves, so I’m delighted that they’ve finally got evidence of that.”

For more than three decades, discoveries in the Côa valley have helped to reshape the perception of Palaeolithic rock art from something produced exclusively in caves for ritual purposes to something that was often outdoor and multifunctional. “The vast majority of it was in the open air, and the stuff in caves was almost a marginal phenomenon,” says Bahn. “It just happens to have survived much better.”

To truly understand such art, though, Aubry says we must stop studying it as a distinct phenomenon and view it instead as an integrated component of the everyday world of ancient hunter-gatherers. “Archaeologists need to realise that we are not studying a monument,” he says. “We are studying people living in a space.”

articles.personality_title: New discovery reveals how ancient hunter-gatherers lived with rock art in Portugal
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Côa valley in Portugal is home to the world’s largest open-air collection of Paleolithic rock art, with carvings that are about 26,000 years old. These ancient drawings show animals and have puzzled archaeologists for years about how they were used by prehistoric people.

**What happened** – Archaeologists led by Thierry Aubry recently found tiny stone tools and signs of campfires right next to animal carvings at the Penascosa site in the Côa valley. These tools are about 26,000 years old and show that hunter-gatherers lived and worked near the rock art. This is the first time such old tools were found so close to the art, proving that the carvings were part of daily life, not just special or sacred places.

**Impact** – This discovery changes how we understand prehistoric people. It shows they used rock art as a way to share stories, practical hunting information, and to connect with other groups. The tools found came from faraway places, suggesting the Côa valley was a meeting point for different bands of hunter-gatherers. The art was not just decoration but a shared language between groups who hunted and lived nearby.

**What’s next step** – Researchers will continue digging to learn more about how people lived and used the rock art. They hope to find more evidence of camps and tools to better understand the social life of these ancient communities. This could lead to new discoveries about how early humans communicated and cooperated across large areas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Archaeologists found 26,000-year-old tools near rock art in Portugal’s Côa valley, showing that prehistoric hunter-gatherers lived among the carvings and used them to share stories and hunting knowledge.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une découverte révèle comment les chasseurs-cueilleurs vivaient avec l’art rupestre au Portugal
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La vallée du Côa au Portugal abrite la plus grande collection d’art rupestre paléolithique en plein air au monde, avec des gravures âgées d’environ 26 000 ans. Ces dessins anciens représentent des animaux et ont longtemps intrigué les archéologues sur leur utilisation par les peuples préhistoriques.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des archéologues dirigés par Thierry Aubry ont récemment trouvé de petits outils en pierre et des traces de feux de camp juste à côté des gravures animales sur le site de Penascosa dans la vallée du Côa. Ces outils datent d’environ 26 000 ans et montrent que les chasseurs-cueilleurs vivaient et travaillaient près de l’art rupestre. C’est la première fois que des outils aussi anciens sont découverts si près des gravures, prouvant que ces œuvres faisaient partie de la vie quotidienne, et pas seulement des lieux sacrés.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change notre compréhension des hommes préhistoriques. Elle montre qu’ils utilisaient l’art rupestre pour raconter des histoires, transmettre des informations pratiques sur la chasse et se connecter avec d’autres groupes. Les outils trouvés venaient de régions lointaines, ce qui suggère que la vallée du Côa était un point de rencontre pour différents groupes de chasseurs-cueilleurs. L’art n’était pas seulement décoratif, mais un langage commun entre les groupes qui chassaient et vivaient à proximité.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont continuer les fouilles pour en apprendre davantage sur la vie autour de l’art rupestre. Ils espèrent trouver plus de preuves de campements et d’outils pour mieux comprendre la vie sociale de ces anciennes communautés. Cela pourrait mener à de nouvelles découvertes sur la communication et la coopération des premiers humains sur de grandes distances.

**Phrase clé** – Des archéologues ont trouvé des outils vieux de 26 000 ans près d’art rupestre dans la vallée du Côa au Portugal, montrant que les chasseurs-cueilleurs préhistoriques vivaient parmi les gravures et les utilisaient pour partager histoires et savoirs de chasse.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo descubrimiento revela cómo vivían los cazadores-recolectores con el arte rupestre en Portugal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El valle del Côa en Portugal alberga la mayor colección de arte rupestre paleolítico al aire libre del mundo, con grabados que tienen unos 26,000 años. Estas antiguas imágenes muestran animales y han desconcertado a los arqueólogos sobre cómo las usaban las personas prehistóricas.

**Qué pasó** – Arqueólogos liderados por Thierry Aubry encontraron recientemente pequeñas herramientas de piedra y señales de fogatas justo al lado de los grabados de animales en el sitio Penascosa, en el valle del Côa. Estas herramientas tienen unos 26,000 años y muestran que los cazadores-recolectores vivían y trabajaban cerca del arte rupestre. Es la primera vez que se encuentran herramientas tan antiguas tan cerca del arte, demostrando que las imágenes formaban parte de la vida diaria, no solo de lugares especiales o sagrados.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento cambia cómo entendemos a los pueblos prehistóricos. Muestra que usaban el arte rupestre para contar historias, compartir información práctica para la caza y conectarse con otros grupos. Las herramientas encontradas venían de lugares lejanos, sugiriendo que el valle del Côa era un punto de encuentro para diferentes bandas de cazadores-recolectores. El arte no era solo decoración, sino un lenguaje común entre grupos que cazaban y vivían cerca.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores continuarán excavando para aprender más sobre cómo vivían y usaban el arte rupestre. Esperan encontrar más evidencias de campamentos y herramientas para entender mejor la vida social de estas antiguas comunidades. Esto podría llevar a nuevos descubrimientos sobre la comunicación y cooperación de los primeros humanos a grandes distancias.

**Frase clave** – Arqueólogos encontraron herramientas de 26,000 años junto al arte rupestre en el valle del Côa en Portugal, mostrando que los cazadores-recolectores prehistóricos vivían entre las grabaciones y las usaban para compartir historias y conocimientos de caza.

articles.title: Inside the New York ‘time machine’ racing to save a century of sound and film
articles.summary: “I tell my kids I work in a time machine,” said Rhony Dostaly. In a basement beneath Lincoln Center, the media preservation engineer rescues moments from the past. “I go back in time, and I grab elements, and I make them available for people today.”
articles.content:
He and his colleagues at the New York Public Library (NYPL) are working against the clock to preserve the contents of film, tape, discs and cylinders that hold more than a century of sound and moving images.

The records are decaying, and the machines that can play them are disappearing.

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

Learning from the past

For Mr. Dostaly, it’s not just about technology. He has watched other people’s lives unfold through the archive.

Harry Belafonte, the legendary American singer, actor, civil rights activist – and longtime UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador – filmed his family for decades, from teaching his son to ride a bike in Central Park to trips abroad.

“I’ve actually seen his kids from toddlers all the way to adults,” Mr. Dostaly said.

© UNICEF/Mariella Furrer

Films of the African American civil rights leader Malcolm X’s travels, including footage from Mecca, moved him the most. “I’m the one who’s going to be making it available for everyone to see,” he remembered thinking.

By looking through footage like this – he hopes – young people “will realize the importance of events that took place before they were here on Earth.”

Cultural heritage

Next door, Casey McNamara, a media preservation coordinator, bends over a reel of film with a jeweller’s loupe or magnifying glass, checking it frame by frame for tears, splices and shrinkage.

On the white leader she has written “BHARATA NATYAM,” the name of one of the oldest Indian classical dance forms.

Films may reach her “in a rusty tin, on an old projection reel, or in a rag box, in plastic bags.” Without the work she does, some collections “would remain mostly unseen.”

The lab is part of NYPL’s Digital Collections Operations. Once digitized, most of the material will be accessible to anyone with a library card.

“The tapes and the decks are no longer being manufactured, but the history needs to be preserved,” explained lab manager Shahed Dowlatshahi.

Work like this is exactly the kind of project that the UN’s World Day for Audiovisual Heritage, marked annually on 27 October, is designed to highlight and assist.

Preserving UN history

In the audio room, Jeffrey Willens slides a 16-inch disc from a brown paper sleeve marked: A Year To Remember.

The UN Radio Division produced it for broadcast on New Year’s Day 1949, when the Organization was still headquartered at Lake Success on Long Island.

Copies would have been mailed to radio stations and UN offices around the world. Mr. Willens places it on a turntable with a microscope mounted above it, and the voices of actor Fredric March and sportscaster Ted Husing fill the room.

Down the corridor, engineers are digitizing the archive of William Greaves, a pioneering African American documentary filmmaker.

His 2001 film Ralph Bunche: An American Odyssey tells the story of the American diplomat who won the 1950 Nobel Peace Prize for mediating the armistice agreements between Israel and Arab States.

Mr. Bunche was the first Black Nobel laureate and later became UN Under-Secretary-General.

‘Kind of like surgery’

Time is working against all of it.

The acetate film which the New York Public Library is trying to preserve suffers from “vinegar syndrome,” a chemical decay that leaves it brittle, warped and smelling of vinegar.

“Once that process starts, there’s no stopping it,” Ms. McNamara said. “You can slow it down with cold storage, but it will never reverse.”

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

Audiotape can arrive crinkled or stuck together and must be repaired by hand. “To be able to repair it and then play it and get a successful transfer is kind of like surgery,” said media preservation engineer Victoria Fajardo. “It really is such a privilege to be one of the first people to listen to a lot of this content for the first time since it’s been recorded.”

Even Digital Betacam cassettes, once considered robust, have started to shed. Francis Dougherty, the specialist who originally built the video lab, now has to clean his deck between tapes. “Every year this job gets more difficult,” he said. “Every year physical media degrades.”

The last of the repairmen

“The machines are getting rarer,” Mr. Dougherty added. “The old men who repair the machines are getting even rarer.”

UN News/Evgeniya Kleshcheva

Asked how urgent the work is, he does not hesitate: “It should have been dealt with 20 years ago.”

Universities train young specialists but there are fewer and fewer machines for them to work on.

“Without people to maintain and repair and service them, we won’t be able to do this,” Mr. Dowlatshahi added. “And there’s only a few people that do it now.”

Work in progress

Some solutions are built by hand. The turntable that played the UN disc was made by Nick Bergh, a California engineer who builds playback machines as “sort of a hobby.” The library has one of the first in the world.

It isn’t even finished. For now, its microscope lets engineers inspect record grooves for scratches; eventually, a second arm will read discs optically, without touching them.

Bergh’s earlier machine uses lasers to align warped wax cylinders to within microns and to read broken ones without contact.

The library used it to re-transfer the Mapleson Cylinders, recorded at the Metropolitan Opera in the early 1900s. They hold “unique performances by singers who were never otherwise recorded.”

The paradox according to Mr. Willens is that as playback technology improves, the original recordings keep deteriorating.

Every year of waiting means less heritage left to save.

articles.personality_title: New York Library races to save a century of sound and film history
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
The New York Public Library is working to save old sound recordings and films that are more than 100 years old. These recordings are stored on tapes, discs, and film reels that are slowly breaking down and becoming unusable. At the same time, the machines needed to play these recordings are disappearing.

**What happened**
A team of media preservation experts, including Rhony Dostaly and Casey McNamara, is carefully repairing and digitizing these fragile materials in a special lab beneath Lincoln Center. They handle everything from old films of famous people like singer Harry Belafonte and civil rights leader Malcolm X to historic United Nations recordings from the 1940s. They use tools like microscopes and custom-built machines to fix and copy the recordings into digital formats.

**Impact**
This work saves important moments from history that would otherwise be lost forever. For example, the team has preserved rare performances from early 1900s opera and films that show important events and people. By digitizing the materials, the library makes them available to anyone with a library card, helping people learn about history through real voices and images. The project also highlights the challenge of preserving culture as both the recordings and playback machines age and disappear.

**What's next step**
The team will continue digitizing more collections and improving their equipment. Engineers are building new machines to play old discs without damaging them and to restore broken recordings. However, experts warn that time is running out because the materials keep deteriorating and fewer people know how to repair the old machines. Training new specialists and creating more tools will be important to keep saving this cultural heritage.

**One-sentence takeaway**
The New York Public Library is urgently preserving and digitizing fragile sound and film recordings to protect over a century of cultural history for future generations.
articles.personality_title_fr: La bibliothèque de New York sauve un siècle d’histoire sonore et cinématographique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
La Bibliothèque publique de New York travaille à sauver de vieux enregistrements sonores et films datant de plus de 100 ans. Ces enregistrements sont stockés sur des bandes, disques et bobines qui se détériorent lentement. En même temps, les machines nécessaires pour les lire disparaissent.

**Ce qui s’est passé**
Une équipe d’experts en préservation des médias, dont Rhony Dostaly et Casey McNamara, répare et numérise soigneusement ces matériaux fragiles dans un laboratoire sous le Lincoln Center. Ils traitent des films anciens de personnalités comme le chanteur Harry Belafonte et le leader des droits civiques Malcolm X, ainsi que des enregistrements historiques des Nations Unies des années 1940. Ils utilisent des microscopes et des machines fabriquées sur mesure pour restaurer et copier les enregistrements en format numérique.

**Impact**
Ce travail permet de sauver des moments importants de l’histoire qui auraient été perdus. Par exemple, l’équipe a préservé des performances rares d’opéra du début des années 1900 et des films montrant des événements et personnes marquants. En numérisant ces matériaux, la bibliothèque les rend accessibles à toute personne ayant une carte de bibliothèque, aidant ainsi à apprendre l’histoire à travers des voix et images réelles. Ce projet montre aussi le défi de préserver la culture alors que les enregistrements et les machines vieillissent.

**Prochaine étape**
L’équipe continuera à numériser d’autres collections et à améliorer son équipement. Des ingénieurs construisent de nouvelles machines pour lire les vieux disques sans les abîmer et pour restaurer les enregistrements cassés. Cependant, les experts préviennent que le temps presse car les matériaux se détériorent et les spécialistes capables de réparer les anciennes machines se font rares. Former de nouveaux experts et créer plus d’outils sera important pour continuer à sauver ce patrimoine culturel.

**Phrase clé**
La Bibliothèque publique de New York préserve en urgence des enregistrements sonores et films fragiles afin de protéger plus d’un siècle d’histoire culturelle pour les générations futures.
articles.personality_title_es: La biblioteca de Nueva York salva un siglo de historia sonora y cinematográfica
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
La Biblioteca Pública de Nueva York está trabajando para salvar viejas grabaciones de sonido y películas de más de 100 años. Estas grabaciones están en cintas, discos y rollos de película que se están deteriorando poco a poco. Al mismo tiempo, las máquinas necesarias para reproducirlas están desapareciendo.

**Qué pasó**
Un equipo de expertos en preservación de medios, incluyendo a Rhony Dostaly y Casey McNamara, está reparando y digitalizando cuidadosamente estos materiales frágiles en un laboratorio bajo Lincoln Center. Manejan desde películas antiguas de personas famosas como el cantante Harry Belafonte y el líder de derechos civiles Malcolm X, hasta grabaciones históricas de las Naciones Unidas de los años 40. Usan herramientas como microscopios y máquinas hechas a medida para reparar y copiar las grabaciones en formato digital.

**Impacto**
Este trabajo salva momentos importantes de la historia que de otro modo se perderían para siempre. Por ejemplo, el equipo ha preservado actuaciones raras de ópera de principios del siglo XX y películas que muestran eventos y personas importantes. Al digitalizar el material, la biblioteca lo hace accesible a cualquier persona con una tarjeta de biblioteca, ayudando a aprender historia a través de voces e imágenes reales. El proyecto también muestra el desafío de preservar la cultura a medida que las grabaciones y las máquinas envejecen.

**Próximo paso**
El equipo continuará digitalizando más colecciones y mejorando su equipo. Los ingenieros están construyendo nuevas máquinas para reproducir discos viejos sin dañarlos y para restaurar grabaciones rotas. Sin embargo, los expertos advierten que el tiempo se acaba porque los materiales siguen deteriorándose y cada vez hay menos personas que saben reparar las máquinas antiguas. Formar nuevos especialistas y crear más herramientas será importante para seguir salvando este patrimonio cultural.

La Biblioteca Pública de Nueva York está preservando urgentemente grabaciones sonoras y películas frágiles para proteger más de un siglo de historia cultural para las futuras generaciones.

articles.title: The portraits that helped bring the lost Aberfan children home
articles.summary: An artist living hundreds of miles away felt compelled to help the village that lost its children.
articles.content:
For almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village.

Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique.

The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings.

In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits, some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve.
articles.reasoning: The story highlights a meaningful artistic initiative that helped a community heal from a tragic event by preserving the memory of lost children through portraits, providing emotional comfort and connection to many families over decades. It has broad emotional and cultural significance beyond a small niche.

articles.title: Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
articles.summary: Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred, and sometimes discarded their dogs.
articles.content:
Archaeologists working at an ancient burial complex in Peru have uncovered remarkable evidence of hairless dogs that lived more than 1,200 years ago, long before the rise of the Inca Empire. The discoveries include naturally mummified remains, unusual skeletal features, and clues about what the animals ate and how they were treated by the people around them.

Peruvian hairless dogs are a distinctive Indigenous breed known for their slender bodies, pointed ears, and lack of fur. They frequently appear in pottery created by ancient societies along the Andean coast. Today, a variation of the breed is recognized by the American Kennel Club as the Peruvian Inca Orchid. The dogs are also an important national symbol, having been officially designated part of Peru's cultural heritage in 2000.

A study published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology reports the first physical evidence of Peruvian hairless dogs at Castillo de Huarmey, the only known Wari Empire site discovered so far on Peru's northern coast.

Ancient Dog Remains Discovered at a Wari Empire Site

Located approximately 190 miles north of Lima, Castillo de Huarmey covers 110 acres and once served as an administrative and burial center for the Wari Empire. The complex was occupied between 600 and 1050 CE, roughly 400 years before the Inca rose to power.

The site has already produced several extraordinary archaeological discoveries. In 2012, researchers uncovered the first undisturbed elite Wari tomb, containing the remains of 58 high-status women, six human sacrifices, and approximately 1,300 artifacts. Another important discovery followed in 2022, when archaeologists identified nearby burials of elite craftspeople accompanied by gold, silver, and bronze tools. Together, these findings have helped researchers understand how the Wari Empire governed its territories.

The newly examined dog remains offer a different perspective on daily life at the site, particularly the complicated relationships between people and animals.

"Our findings indicate that humans and dogs coexisted at this Wari site, but reconstructing their bond is challenging, as past emotions are difficult to capture through archaeological methods," says first author Weronika Tomczyk, a research associate in Dartmouth's Department of Anthropology and a postdoctoral fellow in its Ecology, Evolution, Environment and Society Program.

"The goal of our study was to not only present data on Castillo de Huarmey's dog burials, but also emphasize that people in the past had often contradictory relationships with the animals, just as they do today: a pet for one group of people could at the same time be considered a pest by their closest neighbors."

Remarkably Preserved Dog Mummies Found in the Peruvian Desert

Castillo de Huarmey lies in an extremely dry region of Peru's Pacific coast. The desert's exceptionally arid conditions have helped preserve materials that would normally deteriorate over time, including hair, bones, clothing, leather, pigments, and decorated pottery.

Among the artifacts recovered from the site is an unusual ceramic vessel depicting a seated Peruvian hairless dog with humanlike features. The animal appears to be holding an object resembling a musical instrument.

Between 2010 and 2025, excavations also uncovered numerous remains of South American camelids, probably domesticated llamas and alpacas. Some may have been deposited as offerings during funerary ceremonies, while others appear to have been discarded as waste. Archaeologists also recovered the skeletal remains of dogs.

However, interpreting these discoveries has been complicated by extensive damage and looting. A powerful earthquake in 1970 caused part of Castillo de Huarmey to collapse, exposing burial chambers containing pottery and other valuable objects. Looters subsequently disturbed large sections of the complex.

The deeper archaeological layers remained untouched and retained their original Wari context. In contrast, the upper layers, where most of the animal remains were discovered, contained materials that had become mixed together.

During excavations in the northern section of the main ceremonial area, three sets of dog remains stood out.

One was a naturally mummified skull that still retained visible hairless skin and attached ears. The skull had also been colored with cinnabar, a bright red pigment commonly used in ancient Peruvian funerary traditions.

Researchers discovered a second, larger dog skull, along with the naturally mummified skeleton of a male dog buried in a shallow pit. The male skeleton was almost complete, missing only the lower portions of its front limbs.

At first, the researchers suspected that the mummified dog might have been buried relatively recently, perhaps around 50 years earlier during the period of looting. But Tomczyk noticed two important details: the animal was hairless, and all three dogs lacked their first premolars.

Missing Teeth Reveal the Dogs' Ancient Identity

The missing teeth provided an unexpected clue that helped researchers identify the animals.

"What I noticed is that some of the dog skeletons were missing teeth, and not that they lost them during their lifespan; some teeth, especially first premolars and sometimes last molars, had just never erupted," said Tomczyk. "And then I found in the literature that the same gene which is responsible for hairlessness in dogs is responsible for a reduced number of teeth, indicating that these were Peruvian hairless dogs."

In other words, the animals were not necessarily missing teeth because of injury, disease, or old age. Their reduced number of teeth was linked to the same genetic trait responsible for their hairlessness.

This distinctive biological connection offered evidence that the remains belonged to Peruvian hairless dogs rather than other ancient dog populations.

To investigate further, the researchers applied standard zooarchaeological techniques, which involve studying animal remains recovered from archaeological sites. These methods helped them estimate the ages of the dogs and examine their physical characteristics.

The team also analyzed chemical signatures preserved in the animals' bones and teeth. Known as isotopic analysis, this technique can reveal information about what an animal ate and drank, as well as where it may have lived.

The researchers examined isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and strontium. These are different forms of chemical elements that can preserve clues about diet and environmental conditions. Strontium is particularly useful because its composition varies with local geology and can help scientists trace an animal's geographic origins or movements.

The results were compared with similar measurements from human and camelid remains recovered at Castillo de Huarmey.

"Isotopic analyses of a dog's tooth give a signal of its life as a puppy because dog teeth erupt so fast, and the bone gives a signal of more or less the last year of its life," said Tomczyk. "Such sampling strategy aimed to provide signals from distinct stages of a dog's life."

Ancient Puppies Buried Alongside Elite Members of Society

Altogether, the excavations produced 341 dog bone specimens representing at least 19 individual dogs, in addition to the complete mummified male dog.

Some of the remains were found in particularly intriguing burial contexts.

For example, the bones of a puppy estimated to have been just 6 to 8 weeks old were discovered alongside an elite craftsperson nicknamed the "Master Basketmaker." Other finds included the bones of an adult dog buried within the site's palace and part of a puppy skeleton buried with a male individual identified as XY, who was probably sacrificed to serve as a tomb guardian.

Most of the dogs were adults at the time of burial. However, their remains suggest that the animals did not all receive the same treatment.

Some appear to have been deliberately buried, potentially reflecting a special role in Wari society. Others were found among discarded materials. Only a small number of bones displayed butchery marks, suggesting that dogs were not commonly consumed as food.

Radiocarbon dating provided another important discovery. The complete mummified male dog was determined to be at least 1,200 years old, making it the oldest radiocarbon-dated specimen recovered from Castillo de Huarmey so far.

This result has important implications for understanding the site's chronology because it provides an additional dating reference for the ancient complex.

Ancient Hairless Dogs May Have Eaten Like Humans

The isotopic evidence also revealed surprising similarities between the diets of dogs and people living at Castillo de Huarmey.

Most of the dogs had consumed at least some maize, or corn, which was a major food source throughout the pre-Hispanic Andes. Their diets therefore overlapped with those of the human population.

An especially interesting pattern emerged among the dogs believed to have been hairless.

When these animals were puppies, their diets appeared more similar to those of human children. As they grew older, however, their food sources became more varied.

The findings raise the possibility that some puppies received particular attention or were raised under controlled conditions, potentially as part of an organized breeding practice.

"We do not know if the dogs were intentionally fed maize or if perhaps, they were just eating leftovers or trash," said Tomczyk. "Yet, the distinct dietary patterns of hairless puppies provide insights into what may have been organized breeding."

The researchers emphasize that the archaeological evidence cannot establish whether these dogs were cherished pets, working animals, or animals with other roles in Wari society.

Nevertheless, the differences in burial practices, physical characteristics, and dietary patterns suggest that the hairless dogs held a distinctive place within the community.

"While we will never know if any of the three dogs were pets or how people treated them, it is evident they received different treatment than other dogs," said Tomczyk.

The discoveries provide a rare glimpse into the lives of dogs and humans more than a millennium ago, showing that relationships with animals could be just as varied and complicated in ancient societies as they are today.

The study's co-authors include Miłosz Giersz, Wiesław Więckowski, and Roberto Pimentel Nita of the University of Warsaw, along with Claire Ebert of the University of Pittsburgh.

articles.personality_title: Archaeologists uncover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dogs in Peru
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**
Archaeologists have been studying an ancient burial site in Peru called Castillo de Huarmey, which belonged to the Wari Empire, a civilization that existed about 1,200 years ago. This site has already revealed important information about the people who lived there, including their tools and burial customs.

**What happened**
Researchers found the remains of hairless dogs naturally preserved as mummies at this dry desert site. These dogs were buried alongside humans, including puppies and adult dogs. Scientists noticed the dogs were missing certain teeth, a trait linked to the same gene that causes hairlessness. By studying the bones and teeth, they learned about the dogs’ diets and how they might have been cared for by ancient people.

**Impact**
This discovery is the first physical proof that the famous Peruvian hairless dogs lived during the Wari Empire, long before the Inca. The dogs’ diets showed they ate some of the same foods as humans, like maize (corn), hinting at close relationships. The way some puppies were buried with important people suggests these dogs had special roles, possibly as pets or companions, revealing complex bonds between humans and animals in ancient times.

**What's next step**
Scientists will continue to study these dog remains and compare them with other findings to better understand how ancient Peruvians bred and treated these animals. This could help uncover more about daily life in the Wari Empire and how these dogs became an important part of Peru’s culture.

**One-sentence takeaway**
Ancient mummified hairless dogs found in Peru show that people and their pets had close and varied relationships over 1,200 years ago during the Wari Empire.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des archéologues découvrent des chiens chauves momifiés vieux de 1 200 ans au Pérou
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**
Des archéologues étudient un ancien site funéraire au Pérou appelé Castillo de Huarmey, qui appartenait à l'empire Wari, une civilisation datant d'environ 1 200 ans. Ce site a déjà révélé des informations importantes sur les habitants, leurs outils et leurs coutumes funéraires.

**Ce qui s’est passé**
Les chercheurs ont découvert les restes de chiens chauves naturellement momifiés dans ce désert sec. Ces chiens ont été enterrés aux côtés d’humains, y compris des chiots et des chiens adultes. Les scientifiques ont remarqué que ces chiens avaient certaines dents manquantes, un trait lié au même gène qui cause la calvitie. En étudiant les os et les dents, ils ont appris ce que mangeaient ces chiens et comment ils étaient peut-être soignés par les anciens.

**Impact**
Cette découverte est la première preuve physique que les célèbres chiens chauves péruviens vivaient à l’époque de l’empire Wari, bien avant les Incas. Le régime alimentaire des chiens montre qu’ils mangeaient certains des mêmes aliments que les humains, comme le maïs, ce qui suggère des liens étroits. Le fait que certains chiots aient été enterrés avec des personnes importantes laisse penser que ces chiens avaient un rôle spécial, peut-être comme animaux de compagnie, révélant des liens complexes entre humains et animaux dans l’Antiquité.

**Prochaine étape**
Les scientifiques continueront d’étudier ces restes canins et de les comparer avec d’autres découvertes pour mieux comprendre comment les anciens Péruviens élevaient et traitaient ces animaux. Cela pourrait aider à en savoir plus sur la vie quotidienne dans l’empire Wari et sur la place importante de ces chiens dans la culture péruvienne.

**Résumé en une phrase**
Des chiens chauves momifiés vieux de plus de 1 200 ans montrent que les humains et leurs animaux avaient des relations proches et variées à l’époque de l’empire Wari.
articles.personality_title_es: Arqueólogos descubren perros calvos momificados de 1,200 años en Perú
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**
Arqueólogos han estado estudiando un antiguo sitio de entierro en Perú llamado Castillo de Huarmey, que perteneció al Imperio Wari hace unos 1,200 años. Este lugar ya ha revelado información importante sobre las personas que vivían allí, incluyendo sus herramientas y costumbres funerarias.

Qué pasó
Los investigadores encontraron restos de perros calvos momificados de forma natural en este sitio desértico seco. Estos perros fueron enterrados junto a humanos, incluyendo cachorros y perros adultos. Los científicos notaron que a estos perros les faltaban ciertos dientes, un rasgo ligado al mismo gen que causa la calvicie. Al estudiar los huesos y dientes, aprendieron sobre la dieta de los perros y cómo podrían haber sido cuidados por las personas antiguas.

Impacto
Este descubrimiento es la primera prueba física de que los famosos perros calvos peruanos vivieron durante el Imperio Wari, mucho antes del Imperio Inca. Las dietas de los perros mostraron que comían algunos de los mismos alimentos que los humanos, como el maíz, lo que indica relaciones cercanas. La forma en que algunos cachorros fueron enterrados con personas importantes sugiere que estos perros tenían roles especiales, posiblemente como mascotas, mostrando vínculos complejos entre humanos y animales en tiempos antiguos.

Próximo paso
Los científicos seguirán estudiando estos restos de perros y los compararán con otros hallazgos para entender mejor cómo los antiguos peruanos criaban y trataban a estos animales. Esto podría ayudar a descubrir más sobre la vida diaria en el Imperio Wari y cómo estos perros se convirtieron en una parte importante de la cultura peruana.

Conclusión en una frase
Perros calvos momificados encontrados en Perú muestran que hace más de 1,200 años, durante el Imperio Wari, las personas y sus mascotas tenían relaciones cercanas y variadas.
